items.text: What two parts does every argument have, in the logician's sense of the word?
A conclusion (the claim being argued for) and at least one premise (a reason offered for believing the conclusion). A sentence with no reason attached is just an assertion, not an argument.
List the common premise-indicator words (words that flag a reason is coming).
Since, because, given that, for, as, in light of, after all, this is so because.
List the common conclusion-indicator words (words that flag the main point is coming).
Therefore, thus, so, hence, it follows that, as a result, consequently, which means, this shows that.
Is the conclusion of an argument always the last sentence in the paragraph?

No. The conclusion is whatever the premises are trying to establish, and it can sit first, last, or in the middle. Find it by asking what the other statements are offered as support for, not by reading order.

"Since the moisture meter read above 17 percent on three studs, and since Category 2 water sat in that wall for more than 48 hours, the drywall and insulation in that section must be removed." Identify the premises and the conclusion.
Premises (both flagged by "since"): the meter read above 17 percent on three studs, and Category 2 water sat for more than 48 hours. Conclusion: the drywall and insulation must be removed.
"This contractor replaced forty roofs last year. He's the right guy for your job." Is this an argument even though it has no indicator words?

Yes. Test it by inserting "therefore" between the sentences without changing the meaning: it works, so it is an argument, just an undressed one. Premise: replaced forty roofs last year. Conclusion: he's the right guy for the job.
What is the fast test for whether two sentences form an argument at all, when no indicator words are present?

Try inserting "therefore" between the sentences. If the meaning still holds, the first sentence is a premise and the second is a conclusion (or vice versa); if inserting it changes or breaks the meaning, you may just have two unrelated assertions.
A DFS analyst writes: "This running back will likely bust this week, since his offensive line is banged up and the opposing defense ranks third against the run." Diagram it.

Premises (flagged by "since"): the offensive line is banged up, and the opposing defense ranks third against the run. Conclusion (stated first, but still the conclusion): the running back will likely bust this week.
What is the two-step method for diagramming an argument fast?

First find the conclusion (what the passage is trying to establish). Second, find whatever is offered as support for it (the premises). Doing this in the reverse order, accepting whatever comes last as "the conclusion," is the beginner mistake.
How many conclusions and how many premises does a single argument have, at minimum?

Exactly one conclusion, and at least one premise. An argument can have many premises supporting one conclusion, but if you find yourself naming two separate conclusions, you are looking at two separate arguments stitched together.
What is the "assumption gap" in an argument?
Whatever the argument's conclusion silently depends on beyond its stated premises. Almost no real-world argument states every premise it actually needs to reach its conclusion.
What is the test for finding an argument's hidden assumption?

Ask what would have to be true for the stated premises to actually reach the conclusion, then check whether that thing was ever said. If it was not said, and the argument falls apart without it, that is the assumption.

An adjuster's denial letter says: "The policy requires prompt notice of loss. The insured waited eleven months to report the leak. Therefore the claim is properly denied." What is the unstated assumption?

That waiting eleven months is not prompt notice under this specific policy's actual wording, and that nothing (a discovery rule, a tolling provision, insurer waiver) excuses the delay. The letter asserts the conclusion as if that gap were already closed; it never proves it.
A sales pitch says: "Our dehumidifiers run around the clock in your basement, so your mold risk is zero." What is the unstated assumption, and why is it too strong?

That continuous dehumidification is, by itself, sufficient to eliminate mold risk entirely, with no role for ventilation, hidden moisture behind walls, or organic material already contaminated. Once stated out loud, the assumption is obviously too strong for the premise to carry.
A trader says: "This stock gapped up on high volume this morning, so it's going higher today." What is the unstated assumption?

That a volume-backed gap at the open reliably continues in the same direction through the rest of the day, with no accounting for gap fades, profit-taking, or the move already being priced in. The premise (the gap happened) does not by itself establish the conclusion (it keeps going).
Why does naming the assumption gap matter more than just feeling that an argument is "off"?

Because it turns a vague feeling into a specific, checkable claim. Once the hidden assumption is stated out loud, you can test whether it is actually true, instead of just sensing something is wrong without being able to say what.
What is a conditional statement, and what are its two named parts?
A statement of the form "if A, then B." A is the antecedent (the "if" part), B is the consequent (the "then" part).
What single promise does "if A, then B" make, and what does it say about the case where A is false?
It promises only that whenever A is true, B is true. It says nothing at all about what happens when A is false; B could still be true or false in that case, and the conditional does not address it.

"If the water intrusion is Category 3 (contaminated, black water), then all porous materials in the affected area must be removed." Name the antecedent and the consequent, and what the statement is silent about.

Antecedent: the water is Category 3. Consequent: porous materials must be removed. The statement is silent about Category 1 or 2 water; removal might still be required for another reason (mold, prolonged exposure), or might not be, and this conditional does not say either way.
Given "if A, then B," what is the contrapositive, and is it logically equivalent to the original?

The contrapositive is "if not B, then not A." Yes, it is fully equivalent: whenever the original is true the contrapositive is true, and whenever the original is false the contrapositive is false. It is the one guaranteed, automatic valid rewrite.
Take "if the water is Category 3, then porous materials must be removed." State the contrapositive and check it makes sense.

Contrapositive: if porous materials do not have to be removed, then the water was not Category 3. Checks out: if removal had been required, that would only be because of Category 3 water (per the original), so no required removal means the water was not Category 3.
"If a loss is excluded under the policy, then the carrier does not owe payment." State the contrapositive.

If the carrier owes payment, then the loss was not excluded. A carrier that pays necessarily found no applicable exclusion applied (setting aside waiver, which is a separate doctrine, not a logic issue).
Given "if A, then B," what is the converse, and is it logically equivalent to the original?
The converse is "if B, then A." No, it is not equivalent. The original tells you nothing about whether the converse is true; it can be independently true or false.
"If the water is Category 3, then porous materials must be removed." Why does the converse, "if porous materials must be removed, then the water is Category 3," fail?

Because porous materials can also require removal from a slow Category 1 leak that caused mold growth over several weeks, with no contaminated water involved at all. Removal being required does not pin the cause down to Category 3 water.
Given "if A, then B," what is the inverse, and is it logically equivalent to the original?
The inverse is "if not A, then not B." No, it is not equivalent, for the same reason the converse fails (the inverse is logically identical to the converse's contrapositive).
"If the water is Category 3, then porous materials must be removed." Why does the inverse, "if the water is not Category 3, then porous materials do not have to be removed," fail?
Same counterexample as the converse: a slow, non-Category-3 leak that grew mold over weeks can still force removal. Not having Category 3 water does not guarantee removal is unnecessary.
Give the full map: starting from "if A, then B," which rewrite is valid, and which two are not?
Valid (equivalent): the contrapositive, "if not B, then not A." Not equivalent: the converse, "if B, then A," and the inverse, "if not A, then not B."

A closer says: "If you sign the contract today, you lock in this quoted price." A homeowner hears this as "so if I want to lock in this price, I have to sign today." What logical error did the homeowner just make?

The homeowner silently swapped the original conditional for its converse (if B, then A) and treated it as guaranteed. The original only promised that signing today locks the price; it never said signing today was the only way to lock it. The price might also be available tomorrow.
A sportsbook rule: "If a bet settles as a push, the stake is returned." What does this conditional NOT tell you about a bet whose stake was returned?
It does not tell you the bet was a push. The converse, "if the stake was returned, the bet was a push," is not guaranteed; a canceled or voided bet could also return the stake with no push involved.
Why is it worth memorizing that the converse and inverse are logically identical to each other?

Because once you spot one error you have spotted the other: the inverse of "if A, then B" is just the contrapositive of its converse, "if B, then A." Anyone who falls for one trap is structurally exposed to the other.
Translate "A only if B" into an if-then statement.
"If A, then B." "Only if" marks the necessary condition, and the necessary condition sits on the consequent ("then") side.
"We will start mold remediation only if the moisture meter reads below 15 percent." Translate and verify by substitution.

A = we start remediation, B = the meter reads below 15 percent. Translation: if A, then B. Check: remediation only starts once the threshold clears, so remediation actually happening guarantees the reading was already below 15 percent going in. Matches.
Translate "unless A, B" into an if-then statement.
"If not A, then B." The thing after "unless" is the one condition that would prevent B; its absence triggers B.
"Unless the insured gives notice of loss within the policy's deadline, the claim is barred." Translate and verify by substitution.

A = gives timely notice, B = claim is barred. Translation: if not A, then B. Check: timely notice is the one thing that keeps the bar from kicking in, so its absence (not A) triggers the bar (B). Matches.
"Unless the line moves at least half a point, I'm not touching this bet." Translate.
A = the line moves at least half a point, B = I'm not touching this bet. Translation: if not A, then B (if the line does not move at least half a point, then I'm not touching the bet).
Translate "A is necessary for B" into an if-then statement.
"If B, then A." B cannot happen without A, so B being true guarantees A was already true.
"Being on the active NFL roster, not injured reserve, is necessary for a player to score fantasy points that week." Translate and verify by substitution.

A = on the active roster, B = scores fantasy points. Translation: if B, then A. Check: a player can be active and still score zero, so A does not guarantee B; but scoring any points absolutely requires having been active, so B guarantees A. Matches "if B, then A" only.
"A clean title search is necessary for the lien to be released at closing." Translate.
A = clean title search, B = lien released at closing. Translation: if B, then A (if the lien was released at closing, then the title search was clean).
Translate "A is sufficient for B" into an if-then statement.
"If A, then B." A, by itself, guarantees B; this says nothing about whether A is the only way to get B.
"Signing today is sufficient to lock in this quoted price." Translate and verify by substitution.

A = sign today, B = price is locked. Translation: if A, then B. Check: this is exactly the promise made, that signing today guarantees the lock, with no claim that it's the only way to lock the price. Matches, and is not a promise that B requires A.
"Necessary for" and "sufficient for" look like mirror-image phrases. Do they translate the same direction?

No, they point opposite directions. "A is necessary for B" is "if B, then A." "A is sufficient for B" is "if A, then B." Test each with a real substitution rather than memorizing which phrase "sounds like" which direction.
Translate plain "A if B" (no "only"), and contrast it with "A only if B."

"A if B" translates to "if B, then A" (plain "if" marks a sufficient condition for A). "A only if B" translates to "if A, then B" ("only if" marks a necessary condition for A). Swapping one word for the other flips the entire arrow.

A carrier's handbook says: "A supplemental estimate is reviewed only if it is submitted with photo documentation." A contractor submits photo documentation. Can he conclude his supplement will be reviewed?

No. The translation is "if reviewed, then photo documentation was submitted" (if A, then B), not the reverse. Photo documentation is necessary for review, not sufficient for it; other requirements could still block review. Submitting photos only satisfies one necessary condition.

A trading rule: "A trade is sufficient to count toward your pattern-day-trader status if it is a round-trip in the same margin account on the same day." Does NOT doing a same-day round trip prove the trade does not count toward that status?

Not necessarily, as stated. "Sufficient" translates to "if A, then B," which says nothing about what happens when A is false; some other rule could still make a different trade count. Denying the antecedent here (not A, therefore not B) would be the exact fallacy covered later in this domain.
Define "affirming the consequent" as a formal fallacy.
From "if A, then B" and "B is true," wrongly concluding "A is true." This treats the converse as if it were valid, which it is not.

A policy says: "If a loss is caused by flood, then it is excluded from coverage." An adjuster observes the claim is denied as excluded and writes, "this claim is excluded, so the loss must have been caused by flood." Name and explain the fallacy.

Affirming the consequent. The exclusion (B) being true does not prove the antecedent (flood) was the cause; plenty of other perils (earth movement, wear and tear, intentional acts) are also excluded under the same policy, so being excluded does not pin the cause to flood specifically.
Define "denying the antecedent" as a formal fallacy.
From "if A, then B" and "A is false," wrongly concluding "B is false." This treats the inverse as if it were valid, which it is not.

"If a roof is more than 20 years old, the carrier will require a four-point inspection before binding coverage." A homeowner's roof is 12 years old. He concludes: "so the carrier will not require a four-point inspection." Name and explain the fallacy.

Denying the antecedent. The carrier could still require the inspection for an unrelated reason (a prior claim on the property, a coastal wind zone, an underwriting guideline about a specific roofing material); the 20-year rule says nothing about those cases.

"If a stock beats earnings estimates, the shares typically pop at the open." This stock missed estimates. A trader concludes: "so the shares will not pop at the open." Name the fallacy and a realistic counterexample.

Denying the antecedent. The shares could still pop on other news entirely unrelated to this quarter's earnings number, such as a surprise buyback announcement, a short squeeze, or a sector-wide rally; missing estimates does not rule those out.

"If a player is ruled out on the injury report, he scores zero fantasy points." This player scored zero fantasy points. A DFS player concludes: "so he must have been ruled out." Name the fallacy and a realistic counterexample.

Affirming the consequent. A player can score zero points while active and healthy (a scoreless game, a quick benching, a blowout with no garbage-time work); scoring zero does not prove he was ruled out.
Why do affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent feel airtight in the moment, even though both are invalid?

Because a true conditional is sitting right there in plain sight, and it is easy to mistake a one-directional promise (A guarantees B) for a two-way relationship. Both fallacies are just the converse-and-inverse mistake dressed up as a two-step argument instead of a bare rewrite.

A public adjuster tells a homeowner: "If the roof was damaged by wind, the carrier owes replacement cost. Your roof is damaged, so the carrier owes replacement cost." What is missing before this reasoning is valid, and what would make it affirming the consequent if skipped?

Missing: proof the damage was actually caused by wind (the antecedent), not just that damage exists. If the adjuster instead argued backward from "the carrier paid replacement cost" to "therefore it must have been wind damage," that would be affirming the consequent, since other perils can also trigger replacement cost.

"If you miss the deadline to appeal a claim denial, you lose the right to sue." A policyholder did not miss the deadline. He concludes: "so I definitely still have the right to sue." What is wrong with this, even though the conclusion happens to match the usual case?

It is denying the antecedent: not missing the deadline does not, by itself, guarantee the right to sue, since some other condition (a separate contractual limitation period, a different procedural default) could independently cut off the right to sue. The conditional about the deadline never addressed those other paths.
What single habit protects you from both affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent in a real conversation?

Before accepting any backward inference from a conditional, explicitly check which half of the sentence you actually have (the antecedent or the consequent, affirmed or denied), and remember the conditional makes a promise in one direction only. If you have the consequent, or the negation of the antecedent, the original statement is silent, not helpful.
